subtype: Approach: relies on a lucky routine on exam day [Action]
passage:
Rain was hammering the road when Parth left for the last paper of the term. He had done what he always did: two nights of past-paper questions, a list of formulas pinned above his desk, and the same blue pen in his pocket.
The bus was late, so he ran the last stretch and slowed at the old temple wall. He pressed his palm against the wet stone for two breaths. His shoulders dropped.
"Every time?" Shreya asked, catching up under the shelter.
"Every time," said Parth. "It doesn't do the sums, though."
Inside, he wrote the first answer with the blue pen, steady, and it was the formulas that got him through the question on rates.

qa.q: What does Parth press his palm against before the paper?
qa.a: Parth presses his palm against the wet stone of the old temple wall for two breaths.

qa.q: What does the temple wall do for Parth's mood?
qa.a: It calms him, since his shoulders dropped after two breaths at the wall.

qa.q: What could help Parth stay calm if he could not reach the wall?
qa.a: Parth could take two slow breaths with the blue pen in hand, because the calm seems to come from a short pause, and his real preparation is the past papers and the formulas.

qa.q: How does Shreya seem to see Parth's ritual?
qa.a: Shreya asks 'Every time?' with curiosity, not mockery, and hears Parth say the wall does not do the sums.

grounding: A teenager uses a lucky pen and a wall touch to feel calm on exam day while also studying.

subtype: Approach: expects things to work because they should [Pitfall]
passage:
Ritwik had worked hard for three years: top marks in the lab, a project he was proud of, late nights before every submission. So when the company interview was fixed for Thursday morning, he did not open a single page about the company. Hard work always paid off, he told his roommate, so the interview would go well.
The train was delayed, and he walked in breathless with ten minutes to spare.
"What do you know about our product line?" the panel asked. Then: "How would you approach this case study?" He knew neither. He answered with stories about effort, and the panel nodded politely and wrote very little.

qa.q: Which day was the interview fixed for?
qa.a: The interview was fixed for Thursday morning.

qa.q: What did Ritwik expect about the interview, and why?
qa.a: Ritwik expected it to go well because hard work always paid off, and felt confident enough to skip any preparation.

qa.q: What could Ritwik have done in the days before the interview?
qa.a: Ritwik could have read about the company and practised a sample case study, since the panel asked about those exact things and general effort could not answer them.

qa.q: How might the panel see Ritwik's answers?
qa.a: The panel nodded politely and wrote very little, so they may have seen a hard-working person who had not prepared for their questions.

grounding: A student assumes that working hard in general means the interview will go well and does no preparation.

subtype: Approach: separates comforting rituals from the concrete steps that actually matter [Revision]
passage:
Vandana: You still light the lamp before you sit down?
Rekha: Every morning. Nothing has changed there. It quiets my head.
Vandana: And last attempt you lit it and then read the same chapters again.
Rekha: I know. It felt like preparing. It wasn't. It was comfort.
Vandana: So what's different this time?
Rekha: Lamp first, then a timed mock test every Saturday. Then I sit with you and go through what I missed.
Vandana: You want me to mark them?
Rekha: I want you to tell me what I got wrong, not what I got right.
Vandana: That could be a long list.
Rekha: A list I can work with. The lamp only helps me sit down 🙂

qa.q: How often does Rekha plan a timed mock test?
qa.a: Rekha plans a timed mock test every Saturday.

qa.q: What does Rekha feel about the lamp ritual now?
qa.a: Rekha still finds it calming, since it quiets the head, but knows it was comfort and not preparing. 🙂

qa.q: What else could Rekha use besides mock tests to find weak spots?
qa.a: Rekha could keep a notebook of every wrong answer and revisit it weekly, since a written list shows patterns that comfort alone hides.

qa.q: How might Vandana feel about being asked to mark the mocks?
qa.a: Vandana may feel a little worried about the long list of errors, but also trusted, since Rekha wants honest feedback.

grounding: After a failed attempt, Rekha keeps a calming ritual but adds mock tests and feedback so comfort no longer replaces preparation.

subtype: Approach: puts off an unpleasant task by doing something easy [Pitfall]
passage:
Nikita: Imran, why are there twenty pencils in a row on the table?
Imran: Sharpening them, Didi. Sharp pencils write better.
Nikita: And the bookshelf? It's all in colour order now.
Imran: It was messy.
Nikita: Where's your maths worksheet?
Imran: In my bag.
Nikita: Have you started it?
Imran: The division ones are too hard. I'll do them after the pencils.
Ammi: (from the kitchen) Dinner in ten minutes!
Imran: Already? But I haven't...
Nikita: Look, the pencils are perfect. The page is still blank.
Imran: I know. I'll look at it after dinner.

qa.q: How many pencils are lined up on the table?
qa.a: There are twenty pencils in a row on the table.

qa.q: What might Imran be worried about when saying the division ones are too hard?
qa.a: Imran is probably afraid of the division problems and feels stuck, which is why the pencils and bookshelf come first.

qa.q: What small step could help Imran start the worksheet?
qa.a: Imran could try just the first division question with Didi sitting nearby, since one small try makes the rest feel less scary.

qa.q: How does Nikita see the tidying?
qa.a: Nikita sees perfect pencils and a blank page, and notices that all the tidying has not touched the worksheet.

grounding: Faced with a hard worksheet, a child does easy jobs like tidying and sharpening while the feared task stays untouched.

subtype: Approach: delays because the task feels too big [Thinking]
passage:
I'm Hrithik. This was last month, the day the history essay was assigned. Two thousand words, due in three weeks. I opened my laptop meaning to start, and my thumb found my phone instead. One video, then another. I told myself I'd open the file after this one.
The trouble was, I knew that the moment I opened it I'd see the blank page, and the blank page made me feel small, like the essay was a mountain and I was carrying a spoon. So I didn't open it. Three evenings went like that. The file sat on the desktop and I looked past it every time.

qa.q: How many words was the history essay?
qa.a: The history essay was two thousand words.

qa.q: Why does Hrithik feel small when thinking about the file?
qa.a: Hrithik feels small because the blank page makes the essay seem like a mountain and Hrithik a person carrying a spoon.

qa.q: What could Hrithik try to make the task feel smaller?
qa.a: Hrithik could split the essay into short parts and write a rough opening paragraph first, since a small piece is easier to begin than the whole essay.

qa.q: How might a teacher see the three evenings without progress?
qa.a: A teacher may notice only that no work has begun, without knowing that the size of the task was making Hrithik avoid opening the file.

grounding: A teenager scrolls on a phone and avoids opening a long essay because its size feels overwhelming.

subtype: Approach: starts with two minutes to get going [Revision]
passage:
Writing lab note, Thursday.
Deepak came in again about his lab report, due Monday. He said he had been avoiding it since Tuesday and felt stuck at the very start. I did not tell him what to write. He said himself that he would type a single sentence in the blank document, nothing more, just to begin.
Sitting at the next desk, I watched him write a title sentence, then a second. Then he asked for water and went straight back. When I left an hour later he was still writing, with four paragraphs done. He told me starting was the hard part, not the writing.
I will check in on Saturday.
Zeenat, writing mentor

qa.q: When is Deepak's lab report due?
qa.a: Deepak's lab report is due Monday.

qa.q: What did Deepak feel at the start of the visit?
qa.a: Deepak felt stuck and had been avoiding the report since Tuesday, and found the beginning the hardest part.

qa.q: What could Deepak do on the next report if he feels stuck again?
qa.a: Deepak could set the same small target of one sentence, since the small start got him going once already.

qa.q: How does Zeenat seem to see Deepak's progress?
qa.a: Zeenat stays at the next desk without giving the answer and plans a check-in on Saturday, showing patience and trust in Deepak.

grounding: A student avoiding a report promises himself one sentence to begin, and starting leads to an hour of writing.

subtype: Approach: avoids a difficult conversation and lets the problem grow [Pitfall]
passage:
(Tuesday: Lakshmi notices a wrong discount in the Mehta quote, types a message to Manoj, and deletes it.)
Friday
Manoj: Client just called. The quote and invoice don't match, by a lot.
Lakshmi: Oh no.
Manoj: Do you know anything about this?
Lakshmi: I saw the discount was wrong on Tuesday. I meant to tell you.
Manoj: Tuesday?? I could have fixed it in five minutes then. Now they think we're careless 😕
Lakshmi: I'm sorry. I kept thinking it would be easier tomorrow.
Manoj: Call them with me? Let's do it now.
Lakshmi: Yes 😔

qa.q: What did Lakshmi notice on Tuesday?
qa.a: Lakshmi noticed a wrong discount in the Mehta quote.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi think while putting off the message?
qa.a: Lakshmi kept thinking it would be easier tomorrow, and felt uneasy and sorry that the delay made things worse.

qa.q: What could Lakshmi have done on Tuesday instead?
qa.a: Lakshmi could have sent the message to Manoj at once, since a five-minute fix was possible before the client noticed.

qa.q: How does Manoj feel about hearing this on Friday?
qa.a: Manoj feels frustrated and worried, since the client now thinks the team is careless and the fix could have been quick.

grounding: A colleague delays telling a teammate about a mistake until the client notices, making the conversation harder.

subtype: Approach: names the fear behind the delay and takes a small step [Revision]
passage:
Dear Kamal,
Quick update. For nine days I kept not sending my draft to my manager. Last night I finally asked myself why, and the honest answer was that I'm scared she will say it's weak.
So I wrote three lines: "Attached is a first draft. I'm nervous about it. Please tell me what is unclear." And I pressed send before I could change my mind.
Her reply came within the hour: two useful notes and a thank you. The relief is much bigger than the worry ever was. I can't believe how long I carried it.
Simran

qa.q: How many days did Simran put off sending the draft?
qa.a: Simran kept not sending the draft for nine days.

qa.q: What did Simran realise about the delay?
qa.a: Simran realised the delay came from fear of criticism, being scared the manager would say the draft is weak.

qa.q: What could Simran do next time a draft feels frightening to share?
qa.a: Simran could send a short honest note straight away, since sending it turned out to be far lighter than carrying the worry.

qa.q: How does the manager respond to the draft?
qa.a: The manager replied within the hour with two useful notes and a thank you, so was glad to see it, not disappointed. 😊

grounding: She notices she is afraid of criticism, writes a short honest message, sends it and feels relief.

subtype: Approach: copies a friend's way of doing something [Action]
passage:
After school Mohit watched his friend Sohan pack a cricket kit at the edge of the field behind the kasba market. Sohan's bag was long and deep: pads at the bottom, bat along the side, helmet on top, gloves tucked inside the helmet. It looked so tidy.
That evening Mohit did exactly the same, step by step. His bag was small. The zip would not close, the helmet fell out, and a glove slid under the bed.
On the way to practice Mohit carried the helmet in one hand and the bat under his arm, and reached the field late.

qa.q: Where did Mohit watch Sohan pack the kit?
qa.a: Mohit watched at the edge of the field behind the kasba market.

qa.q: What might Mohit have thought when he saw Sohan's tidy kit?
qa.a: Mohit admired it and wanted the same tidy result, which is why he copied every step.

qa.q: What could Mohit try instead of copying Sohan's order?
qa.a: Mohit could try packing the things that fit his small bag in a different order, since his bag is not long and deep like Sohan's.

qa.q: How might Sohan see Mohit's packing trouble?
qa.a: Sohan's bag is long and deep, so Sohan might be surprised that the same order does not work, and could help Mohit find one that suits the small bag.

grounding: A boy copies a friend's way of packing a cricket kit, which suits the friend's big bag but not his own small one.

subtype: Approach: adopts a topper's study schedule [Pitfall]
passage:
Lalit: You okay? You've yawned three times since first period.
Jagdish: Five am study slot. Day four.
Lalit: Five? You never wake before seven.
Jagdish: The topper does it. The whole class knows. If it works for him, it will work for me.
Lalit: How's the reading going?
Jagdish: I sit up with the book open and my eyes close. I read the same page four times.
Lalit: Did the maths test come back?
Jagdish: Fourteen out of thirty. Last month I got twenty-one.
Lalit: You do your best work at night.
Jagdish: I know. But five am is what toppers do.

qa.q: How many marks did Jagdish get in the maths test?
qa.a: Jagdish got fourteen out of thirty.

qa.q: What does Jagdish want from the five am routine?
qa.a: Jagdish wants to do as well as the topper and believes that if the routine works for the topper it will work for Jagdish, though Jagdish looks tired and unsure.

qa.q: What could Jagdish try instead of the five am slot?
qa.a: Jagdish could keep a night study slot, since Jagdish works best at night, and borrow only the topper's methods that suit him.

qa.q: How does Lalit see the new routine?
qa.a: Lalit notices the yawns and the lower marks and remembers that Jagdish works best at night, so probably sees the routine as a poor fit.

grounding: A teenager copies a topper's five am study routine though the teenager works best at night, ending up sleepy with lower marks.
